title: Config & Environments in the Pipeline: Quick Revision
summary: Quick revision notes on twelve-factor config, dev/staging/prod parity, per-environment configuration, feature flags vs config, ephemeral preview environments and running database migrations safely in CI/CD.

chapters.title: Twelve-Factor Config: The Mental Model
points: Definition: config is everything that varies between deploys (DB URLs, credentials, hostnames, third-party keys); code is what stays identical across deploys
Rule of factor III: store config in environment variables, never in the codebase; one build artifact, many deploys
Litmus test: could the repo be open-sourced right now without leaking a credential? If not, config is leaking into code
Env vars vs config files vs named groups: env vars are granular and language-neutral, while per-env files like config/prod.yml multiply and get committed; avoid grouping vars as 'production'
Mistake: reading ENV in code with silent defaults (e.g. DB_URL or localhost), so prod boots against the wrong database; fail fast on missing required vars at startup

chapters.title: Dev/Staging/Prod Parity
points: Definition: keep environments as similar as possible; the three gaps are time (long deploy cycles), people (devs write, ops deploys) and tools (different backing services)
Fix the gaps: deploy continuously (hours not weeks), devs deploy their own code, and use the same backing service type and version everywhere
Mistake: SQLite in dev and Postgres in prod hides SQL dialect and locking bugs; run real Postgres locally via docker compose
Parity of behaviour, not scale: staging uses same images, same OS and same service versions, but can be smaller in size and data volume
Promote the same immutable image tag dev to staging to prod; never rebuild per environment, because a rebuild is a different artifact

chapters.title: Configuration per Environment
points: Config layering order, lowest to highest precedence: built-in defaults, then config file, then environment variables, then CLI flags
Secrets vs plain config: non-secret config lives in Git or a ConfigMap; secrets live in a secret manager (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager) and are injected at runtime
Injection example: Kubernetes envFrom with configMapRef and secretRef, or docker run --env-file .env.staging; .env files stay gitignored with a committed .env.example
Pipeline variables: scope CI/CD secrets per environment (GitHub Actions environments, GitLab protected variables) so prod secrets are exposed only to prod deploy jobs and masked in logs
Mistake: a NODE_ENV=staging style switch with if env == 'prod' branches in code; prefer explicit settings such as LOG_LEVEL and FEATURE_X, so behaviour is never keyed on an environment name

chapters.title: Feature Flags vs Config
points: Config is set per deploy and needs a restart or redeploy; a feature flag is evaluated at runtime per request or per user, so it can change without a deploy
Flag types: release flag (hide unfinished code, short-lived), ops flag (kill switch), experiment flag (A/B), permission flag (entitlement, long-lived)
Mechanism: the app asks a flag service (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, OpenFeature SDK) with a user context; percentage rollout hashes the user ID so each user stays consistent
Example: if flags.enabled('new-checkout', user): new_flow() else old_flow(); ship dark, ramp 1% to 10% to 100%, then delete the flag
Mistake: flags never removed become tech debt and untested code paths; give each flag an owner and an expiry date, and default to the safe value if the flag service is down

chapters.title: Ephemeral Preview Environments and Migrations in the Pipeline
points: Preview environment: a full short-lived copy of the app spun up per pull request, with its own URL like pr-123.preview.example.com, and destroyed on PR close or merge
Pipeline flow: on PR open, build the image, deploy to namespace pr-123, seed the database, then post the URL on the PR; a PR-closed trigger tears it down, with a TTL job as a fallback
Preview data: use seeded or anonymised data, never a production copy; give each preview its own database or schema, and cap cost via small instance sizes
Migrations in the pipeline: run them as a separate step before the app rollout (a Kubernetes Job, or a release-phase command); never run them from every app instance at boot, as it causes races

Use expand/contract so old and new code both work during rollout: add the nullable column first, deploy, backfill, then drop the old one later. Never rename or drop in the same release; keep migrations forward-only and rollback via a new migration

chapters.title: Cheat Sheet: Config and Environments
points: Config rule: env vars hold anything that differs per deploy; one artifact is promoted unchanged through every environment
Precedence: defaults, then file, then env var, then CLI flag; a missing required var must crash at startup
Parity checklist: same backing service type and version, same image, continuous deploys, devs own their deploys
Secrets: manager plus runtime injection, scoped per environment, .env gitignored and .env.example committed
Config needs a redeploy while a flag is a runtime toggle; ownership and expiry dates stop flag rot
Preview env: per-PR namespace, seeded data, auto-teardown on close, and a TTL as backup
Migrations: a separate pre-deploy job, expand/contract, backward-compatible with the old code, never a destructive change in the same release
